title: Client Requirements & the Target Audience
description: Learn how to interpret a client brief and use audience profiling to shape every design decision.
content_html:
Starting with the Client

Every professional media product begins with a client brief. This is the starting point for any production: a written or verbal document in which the client explains what they need, why they need it, who it is for and what constraints apply. Reading and interpreting a client brief accurately is one of the most practical skills examined in the Cambridge National, because all your practical project work in the course begins with a brief provided by the exam board acting as a simulated client.

What a Client Brief Contains

A well-written brief sets out the purpose of the product (to inform, persuade, entertain or promote), the client requirements in terms of content and format, the target audience the product must reach, the delivery deadline and any budget limits. It may also specify technical requirements — file formats, dimensions, platform — and brand guidelines such as colours, fonts and logo usage. When reading a brief, media creators must identify what is fixed (non-negotiable requirements such as the logo or deadline) and what is open to creative interpretation (tone, layout, imagery). Failing to meet a fixed requirement is a professional failure, regardless of how good the creative work is.

Key Fact

A client brief typically specifies: purpose (inform, persuade, entertain, promote); target audience; content requirements; format and technical specifications; budget; and deadline. All creative decisions must be traceable back to these requirements — if a decision cannot be justified by the brief, it is a risk.

Defining the Target Audience

A target audience is the specific group of people a media product is created for. Defining the target audience precisely is essential because every subsequent design decision — from colour palette to reading level, from platform choice to music genre — should be shaped by who will consume the product. A product that tries to appeal to everyone usually appeals to no one.

Demographics: Profiling the Audience

Media professionals use demographics to describe and profile their audience. Key demographic variables include: age (a children's app and a pension provider's website require very different design approaches); gender (though design should avoid harmful stereotyping, gender can influence platform, tone and content choices); income (a luxury brand communicates differently to a budget supermarket); location (local vs national vs global reach affects language, cultural references and distribution platform); and interests and hobbies (knowing an audience is passionate about sport vs music vs gaming shapes every creative decision). Together these variables allow a media creator to build a detailed picture of their audience — sometimes captured in a written audience profile or persona.

Once a creator has built an audience profile, each creative choice can be tested against it. A website targeting 12-to-15-year-olds might use bold, high-contrast colours, short paragraphs, large touch-friendly buttons and informal language — all justified by the age demographic. A financial services website for adults aged 35-55 with high incomes would use a restrained colour palette, professional typography, longer text blocks and formal language. Platform choice is also demographic: a product for teenagers is more likely to be encountered on TikTok or Instagram than on a printed leaflet. Audience profiling turns abstract demographic data into concrete, defensible design decisions.

Audience Segmentation

Large audiences can be divided into sub-groups through a process called audience segmentation. Rather than treating all viewers or users identically, segmentation allows a media creator — or a client — to tailor different versions of a product (or different campaign messages) to different groups. For example, a streaming service might segment its audience by age and recommend different genres to different groups, or a games company might create a family-friendly version and an adult-rated version of the same franchise. Understanding segmentation helps you explain why a single brand might produce several visually and tonally distinct media products aimed at different sub-audiences.

Key Fact

The five key demographic variables used to profile a target audience are: age, gender, income, location and interests. These directly influence design decisions including colour palette, typography, language register, platform choice and content format.

A very common exam mistake is to identify the target audience correctly but then stop there. Simply writing "the target audience is teenagers" gains very few marks. Examiners want to see the link between the audience profile and specific design choices: "because the target audience is teenagers aged 13-16, the website uses bold colours, informal language and a mobile-first layout, as this age group primarily accesses content on smartphones". Every audience statement should be followed immediately by a design implication. This cause-and-effect chain is what separates Mastering-level answers from Developing-level ones.
exam_tip_html: For any question about client requirements or target audiences, always write in cause-and-effect chains. Do not just identify — connect. A strong answer sounds like: "Because the client brief specifies a target audience of parents with young children (aged 25-40), the designer used pastel colours and rounded fonts to feel approachable and friendly, rather than the bold, high-contrast palette that would be used for a teenage gaming audience." In your practical work, every creative decision in your evidence should reference either the client brief or the audience profile as its justification.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • A client brief sets out the purpose, audience, content requirements, format, budget and deadline for a media product; all creative decisions must be traceable back to it.
  • Target audiences are defined using demographic variables — age, gender, income, location and interests — which directly shape every design decision from colour palette to platform choice.
  • Audience statements must be followed by design implications; simply naming a target audience without linking it to specific creative choices scores minimal marks in the exam.

glossary_terms.definition: A document provided by a client that outlines what they want a media product to achieve, including purpose, audience, content requirements, format, budget and deadline.
The specific needs, preferences and constraints that a client communicates to a media producer when commissioning a media product.
The specific group of people a media product is designed to reach, defined by shared demographic and psychographic characteristics.
Measurable characteristics used to profile an audience, including age, gender, income, location and interests.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is a demographic variable used to profile a target audience?
A) Production budget
B) Age
C) File format
D) Post-production software
State two pieces of information that a client brief typically provides to a media producer.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two distinct correct answers, for example: the purpose of the product (e.g. to promote, inform, entertain) [1]; the target audience [1]; content requirements [1]; the deadline [1]; the budget [1]; technical specifications such as file format or dimensions [1]; brand guidelines such as colours or fonts [1]. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why identifying the target audience is important when planning a media product.
practice_questions.marks: A basic point scores 1 mark (e.g. 'so the designer knows who the product is for'). Development scores 2 marks (e.g. 'knowing the target audience's age group allows the designer to choose an appropriate language register — informal and direct for teenagers, formal and professional for business clients'). A fully developed answer with an applied example scores 3 marks (e.g. add 'for a children's educational app aimed at ages 7-10, this means using simple vocabulary, large touch-friendly buttons and bright, primary colours, which would be inappropriate for a product targeting adult professionals'). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe what is meant by 'audience segmentation'. Give one example of how a media company might use it.
practice_questions.marks:
Description (up to 2 marks): audience segmentation is the process of dividing a large audience into distinct sub-groups based on shared characteristics (e.g. age, interests, income) so that different messages or product versions can be tailored to each group (2 marks for a clear, developed description; 1 mark for a basic statement such as 'splitting the audience into groups').
Example (up to 2 marks): for example, a streaming platform segments its audience by age and recommends animated content and family films to users under 12, while recommending documentaries and crime dramas to adults aged 35-50, increasing engagement for each sub-group (2 marks for a specific, developed example; 1 mark for a vague example). [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
A local gym has provided a brief for a new promotional video. The brief states that the target audience is adults aged 18-35 who are interested in fitness and health, and who primarily use social media on their smartphones.

Discuss how this target audience information should influence the design and production decisions for the promotional video.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): A balanced discussion covering at least two distinct design or production decisions, each clearly linked to a specific demographic detail from the brief. For example: the mobile-first audience means the video should be produced in a vertical (9:16) format for Instagram Reels or TikTok, with text large enough to read on a small screen; the 18-35 age group and fitness interest means dynamic, fast-paced editing with upbeat music rather than slow, corporate-style pacing. Contrast should be present, e.g. noting the tension between keeping the video short enough for social media attention spans (under 60 seconds) and including enough content to be persuasive.
Secure (3-4 marks): Two design decisions identified and linked to the audience profile with some development.
Developing (2 marks): One decision identified with limited audience linkage.
Emerging (1 mark): A vague reference to the target audience. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A media student claims that understanding the target audience is the single most important factor in determining the success of a media product.

Evaluate the extent to which you agree with this claim.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): A balanced evaluation that argues audience understanding is fundamental because it drives every creative decision (format, platform, language, tone, colour, content) and a product that fails to connect with its audience will not achieve its purpose regardless of technical quality; then challenges this with counter-arguments that other factors are equally or more critical in some contexts — such as meeting all client requirements (a product perfectly matched to its audience but late or over budget has failed), or that technical quality and originality can create audience demand (the audience does not always know what it wants until it sees it, as seen in groundbreaking media works). A clear, substantiated judgement is reached.
Secure (5-6 marks): Points on both sides with an attempt at a judgement.
Developing (3-4 marks): Relevant but largely one-sided points.
Emerging (1-2 marks): A basic statement with no evaluation. [8 marks]

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the following is the best definition of a client brief?
options: A report written after a media product is completed
A list of software tools used during production
A document outlining what a client wants a media product to achieve
A set of instructions for editing footage in post-production

knowledge_checks.q: Which demographic variable would most directly influence a designer's choice of platform for distributing a media product?
Dividing a large audience into sub-groups based on shared characteristics is called audience _____.
The five key demographic variables for audience profiling are age, gender, income, location and _____.
Match each demographic variable to the design decision it most directly influences.
right: Use of local cultural references and language
Tone, pricing messaging and visual luxury cues

flashcard_questions.a: A document outlining what the client wants a media product to achieve, including purpose, audience, format, budget and deadline.

flashcard_questions.q: What are the five key demographic variables used to profile a target audience?
flashcard_questions.a: The five key demographic variables are age, gender, income, location and interests, each shaping a different design decision.
The specific group of people a media product is designed to reach.
Dividing a large audience into sub-groups with shared characteristics so different messages can target each group.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the difference between a fixed requirement and an open creative element in a brief?
flashcard_questions.a: Fixed requirements are non-negotiable (e.g. logo, deadline); open elements allow creative interpretation (e.g. tone, imagery).

flashcard_questions.q: Why might a product for teenagers use short paragraphs and informal language?
flashcard_questions.a: Because the age demographic of the target audience shapes appropriate language register and format choices.

flashcard_questions.q: What is an audience profile or persona?
flashcard_questions.a: A written description of the target audience's demographic characteristics used to guide design decisions.

flashcard_questions.q: Which demographic variable would lead a designer to choose social media over print?
flashcard_questions.a: Age, as younger audiences primarily consume content via social media platforms on smartphones.

flashcard_questions.q: What does purpose refer to in a client brief?
flashcard_questions.a: What the product is meant to achieve: to inform, persuade, entertain or promote.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is it a professional failure to miss a fixed client requirement even if the creative work is excellent?
flashcard_questions.a: Because the client has specified a non-negotiable need; ignoring it means the product has not met the brief.

flashcard_questions.q: How does income as a demographic variable affect media design?
flashcard_questions.a: It shapes tone, pricing messaging and visual cues such as luxury imagery versus budget-friendly styling.

flashcard_questions.q: What exam mistake do students make when describing a target audience?
flashcard_questions.a: Naming the audience without linking it to specific design decisions and their justifications.
